sentences.text: This large, ground-dwelling quadrupedal herbivore could also walk on two legs and measured up to 7 meters long and 2 meters high.
Yunnanosaurus had over sixty spoon-shaped teeth that were self-sharpening by wearing against each other during feeding.
The skull of Y. huangi is distinguished by features such as a small external naris, a robust nasal process, and narrow maxillary teeth without denticles.
Y. youngi is distinguished from Y. huangi by having the longest sixth cervical vertebra and tightly fused sacral vertebrae.
Y. robustus is distinguished by the absence of anteroposterior expansion on the astragalus and a dorsoventrally compressed metatarsal IV shaft.
The species Y. youngi reached a length of 13 meters, making it significantly larger than Y. huangi.
Specimen ZMNH-M8739 consists of partial cranial material and an almost complete postcranial skeleton.

This individual possesses characteristic dentition suggesting a potentially unique feeding mechanism, demonstrated by tooth-to-tooth wear facets on mesial maxillary and dentary teeth, and maxillary teeth with coarse serrations.
The genus Yunnanosaurus was first described by C. C. Young in 1942.
A second species, Yunnanosaurus robustus, was described in 1951, and a third, Yunnanosaurus youngi, was named in 2007.
The first skeletons were discovered by Yang Zhongjian in the Sinemurian stage of the Early Jurassic.
The original discovery included over twenty incomplete skeletons and two skulls excavated by Tsun Yi Wang.
A new species, Y. youngi, was described in 2007 by Lü Junchang and colleagues.
A juvenile individual assigned to Y. robustus was described in 2013 by Sekiya et al.
The holotype of Y. youngi was collected in 2000 from terrestrial sediments deposited during the Pliensbachian stage of the early Jurassic, approximately 191 to 183 million years ago.
A juvenile Y. robustus shows tooth-tooth wear facets and coarse serrations, suggesting a unique feeding mechanism.
Dental microwear analysis indicates Yunnanosaurus fed on less tough and fibrous plants than later sauropods.
Recent analyses place Yunnanosaurus in the taxon Massopoda within a clade including Anchisaurus and Jingshanosaurus.
Yunnanosaurus was previously assigned to various taxa including Thecodontosauridae and Plateosauridae.
The parent group of Yunnanosaurus is Sauropodiformes.
Sekiya et al. (2013) differentiated Y. robustus from Y. huangi by describing a juvenile specimen.
They lived in the early Jurassic period, between 199 and 183 million years ago, in what is now Asia.
Type specimens of Y. huangi and Y. robustus were found in the Huangchiatien locality of the Lufeng Formation in Yunnan.
Specimens of Y. huangi and Y. robustus are housed at the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology in Beijing.
Yunnanosaurus shared its environment with ornithischians, other sauropodomorphs, and theropods like Sinosaurus and Eshanosaurus.
Researchers do not consider Yunnanosaurus to be especially close to sauropods in phylogeny because the rest of the animal's body has a clearly "prosauropod" design.
Similarities in tooth shape are not evidence of close phylogenetic relationship but rather an example of evolutionary convergence.
